items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "IPCC".
items.answer: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which assesses climate science for governments
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which assesses climate science for governments. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why deforestation contributes to climate change.
items.answer: Trees store carbon; cutting and burning them releases CO₂ and removes a carbon sink that would otherwise absorb emissions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Trees store carbon; cutting and burning them releases CO₂ and removes a carbon sink that would otherwise absorb emissions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between climate and weather.
items.answer: Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is the average weather over about 30 years or more.
items.markingKey: Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate is the average weather over about 30 years or more. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use IMD temperature data, crop calendars and two studies; graph trends; evaluate data; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use IMD temperature data, crop calendars and two studies; graph trends; evaluate data; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: The data show atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa (NOAA): 1960: 316.9 ppm; 1980: 338.8 ppm; 2000: 369.7 ppm; 2010: 389.9 ppm; 2023: 421.1 ppm. Calculate the average rate of change per year between 1960 and 2010, and per decade.
items.answer: +1.46 ppm per year (+14.6 per decade)

items.stem:
Source A – IPCC report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, Geneva, 2021

The report concluded that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, and that widespread and rapid changes have occurred. It estimated that global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was about 1.1 °C above 1850–1900.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching climate change: the greenhouse effect, the evidence and the causes? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, Geneva, 2021. Purpose: to provide governments with an assessment of climate science. Value: It summarises thousands of peer-reviewed studies and is approved by governments. Limitation: As a consensus summary it may be cautious, and it was published before the most recent data.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, Geneva, 2021. Purpose: to provide governments with an assessment of climate science. Value: It summarises thousands of peer-reviewed studies and is approved by governments. Limitation: As a consensus summary it may be cautious, and it was published before the most recent data. Award up to [4]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Natural factors explain most of the climate change observed since 1950."
items.answer: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate has changed naturally in the past, e.g. ice ages; volcanoes and solar cycles affect temperature. Arguments against: solar output has not increased since 1950 while temperatures have risen; the IPCC concludes it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the climate. Supported judgement: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on climate change: the greenhouse effect, the evidence and the causes produced the question "Is climate change real?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed question with a clear scientific answer Improved: "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed question with a clear scientific answer); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Explain why increasing CO₂ concentrations cause global warming.
items.answer: CO₂ absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation from the Earth's surface, so more CO₂ traps more heat in the lower atmosphere, raising average temperatures.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: CO₂ absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation from the Earth's surface, so more CO₂ traps more heat in the lower atmosphere, raising average temperatures. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The greenhouse effect is harmful in itself." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Without the natural greenhouse effect Earth would average about −18 °C; the problem is the enhanced effect.
items.markingKey: Without the natural greenhouse effect Earth would average about −18 °C; the problem is the enhanced effect. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Keeling Curve and explain what it reveals about evidence of rising CO₂.
items.answer: Charles David Keeling began measuring CO₂ at Mauna Loa in 1958 at about 315 ppm; the record shows a steady rise and seasonal cycle, passing 420 ppm in 2023. Continuous measurement provides clear evidence of human-caused change.
items.markingKey: Context (Charles David Keeling began measuring CO₂ at Mauna Loa in 1958 at about 315 ppm; the record shows a steady rise and seasonal cycle, passing 420 ppm in 2023.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: continuous measurement provides clear evidence of human-caused change. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evidence of rising CO₂.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Natural factors explain most of the climate change observed since 1950." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: climate has changed naturally in the past, e.g. ice ages; volcanoes and solar cycles affect temperature. Counter-arguments: solar output has not increased since 1950 while temperatures have risen; the IPCC concludes it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the climate. Thesis/conclusion: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which agreement in 2023 created a "loss and damage" fund?
items.answer: The COP28 agreement in Dubai (fund agreed at COP27, operationalised at COP28)
items.markingKey: The COP28 agreement in Dubai (fund agreed at COP27, operationalised at COP28). It aims to help vulnerable countries.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Climate change impacts are only in the future." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Impacts are already observed, including heatwaves, glacier loss and coral bleaching.
items.markingKey: Impacts are already observed, including heatwaves, glacier loss and coral bleaching. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why glacial retreat in the Himalayas threatens water supplies.
items.answer: Glaciers feed rivers such as the Ganges and Indus in the dry season; as they shrink, long-term flows will fall, affecting hundreds of millions of people. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Glaciers feed rivers such as the Ganges and Indus in the dry season; as they shrink, long-term flows will fall, affecting hundreds of millions of people. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the impacts of climate change on people and places?
options: How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?
How can we stop climate change?
items.answer: How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: With reference to Tuvalu, explain how it illustrates sea-level rise and migration.
items.answer: With a maximum elevation of about 4.6 m, Tuvalu faces existential threats; in 2023 it signed a treaty with Australia allowing some citizens to migrate. Small island states face loss of territory and forced relocation.
items.markingKey: Context (With a maximum elevation of about 4.6 m, Tuvalu faces existential threats; in 2023 it signed a treaty with Australia allowing some citizens to migrate.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: small island states face loss of territory and forced relocation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to sea-level rise and migration.

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Mia Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, speech at COP26, Glasgow, 1 November 2021

The prime minister of a Caribbean island state told world leaders that a 2 °C rise would be a death sentence for small island states, and called for reform of global finance to help vulnerable countries adapt and recover from climate disasters.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the impacts of climate change on people and places. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Mia Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, speech at COP26, Glasgow, 1 November 2021. Purpose: to urge leaders to act on climate change and climate finance. Value: It expresses the perspective of small island states. Limitation: It is a persuasive speech, not a scientific report.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Mia Mottley, Prime Minister of Barbados, speech at COP26, Glasgow, 1 November 2021. Purpose: to urge leaders to act on climate change and climate finance. Value: It expresses the perspective of small island states. Limitation: It is a persuasive speech, not a scientific report. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A rare and severe event such as a heatwave, flood, drought or tropical storm"?
items.answer: extreme weather event
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of extreme weather event.

items.stem: Distinguish between slow-onset impacts and sudden-onset impacts.
items.answer: Sudden-onset impacts are events such as floods and storms; slow-onset impacts are gradual changes such as sea-level rise and desertification.
items.markingKey: Sudden-onset impacts are events such as floods and storms; slow-onset impacts are gradual changes such as sea-level rise and desertification. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Use tide-gauge and subsidence data, government reports and two studies; compare causes; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use tide-gauge and subsidence data, government reports and two studies; compare causes; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Low-income countries will suffer the most from climate change."
items.answer: Thesis: Low-income countries are generally most vulnerable, but impacts depend on both exposure and capacity to adapt, and poor groups everywhere are at risk.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they are more dependent on agriculture and have fewer resources to adapt; many are in hot, low-lying or drought-prone regions. Counter-arguments: rich countries also face heatwaves, wildfires and flooding, e.g. Europe 2022; within all countries the poorest suffer most. Thesis/conclusion: Low-income countries are generally most vulnerable, but impacts depend on both exposure and capacity to adapt, and poor groups everywhere are at risk. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: By what year has India pledged to reach net zero emissions?
items.markingKey: B. Announced at COP26 in 2021.

items.stem: A student claims: "The Paris Agreement legally forces countries to meet their targets." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Countries must submit and report on NDCs, but the targets themselves are not legally binding.
items.markingKey: Countries must submit and report on NDCs, but the targets themselves are not legally binding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between adaptation and mitigation.
items.answer: Mitigation tackles the causes by reducing emissions; adaptation responds to the effects by reducing vulnerability.
items.markingKey: Mitigation tackles the causes by reducing emissions; adaptation responds to the effects by reducing vulnerability. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the Paris Agreement uses voluntary national pledges.
items.answer: Binding targets had failed to win universal support; voluntary NDCs allowed almost all countries to join, with a review mechanism to raise ambition over time.
items.markingKey: Content: Binding targets had failed to win universal support; voluntary NDCs allowed almost all countries to join, with a review mechanism to raise ambition over time. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Agreement text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Paris Agreement, Article 2, adopted at COP21, Paris, 12 December 2015

The parties agreed to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C, recognising that this would significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching responses to climate change: mitigation, adaptation and international agreements? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the Paris Agreement, Article 2, adopted at COP21, Paris, 12 December 2015. Purpose: to set the goal of international climate action. Value: It is the agreed legal text accepted by almost all countries. Limitation: It sets goals but not binding national targets; it does not show whether action matches the goals.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of the Paris Agreement, Article 2, adopted at COP21, Paris, 12 December 2015. Purpose: to set the goal of international climate action. Value: It is the agreed legal text accepted by almost all countries. Limitation: It sets goals but not binding national targets; it does not show whether action matches the goals. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: A household uses 800 litres of diesel a year (about 2.68 kg CO₂ per litre). A carbon tax of US$ 25/t CO₂ is introduced, and the household cuts its fuel use by 10%. Calculate the household's annual emissions before the cut, its annual carbon tax after the cut, and evaluate the fairness of carbon taxes.
items.answer: 2.14 t CO₂; tax US$ 48.24
items.markingKey: 800 × 2.68 = 2,144 kg = 2.14 t (A1); after cut 1.930 t (M1); × 25 = US$ 48.24 (A1). Evaluation (3): taxes are regressive for low-income households who spend more of their income on energy; revenue can be returned as dividends (as in Canada) or used to support public transport.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Kyoto Protocol"?
options: The 2015 agreement under which countries aim to limit warming to well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C, through nationally determined contributions
The shrinking of glaciers as melting exceeds accumulation
Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, such as solar, wind, hydro and geothermal
The 1997 agreement setting binding targets for developed countries to cut emissions
items.answer: The 1997 agreement setting binding targets for developed countries to cut emissions
items.markingKey: D. "Kyoto Protocol" is the 1997 agreement setting binding targets for developed countries to cut emissions.

items.stem: With reference to Costa Rica's electricity, explain how it illustrates mitigation.
items.answer: Since 2015 Costa Rica has generated over 98% of its electricity from renewable sources, mainly hydro, geothermal and wind. A middle-income country decarbonised its power sector.
items.markingKey: Context (Since 2015 Costa Rica has generated over 98% of its electricity from renewable sources, mainly hydro, geothermal and wind.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a middle-income country decarbonised its power sector. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to mitigation.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How effective has Sweden's carbon tax been in reducing emissions since 1991?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Use Swedish emissions data, tax rates and two studies; compare with GDP growth; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use Swedish emissions data, tax rates and two studies; compare with GDP growth; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Define the term "sustainable resource management".
items.answer: Using resources to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: using resources to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a circular economy and a linear economy.
items.answer: A linear economy takes resources, makes products and throws them away; a circular economy keeps materials in use and designs out waste.
items.markingKey: A linear economy takes resources, makes products and throws them away; a circular economy keeps materials in use and designs out waste. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why countries are trying to diversify their energy mix.
items.answer: Relying on one source, especially imported fossil fuels, creates risks to supply and prices; diversification improves energy security and can reduce emissions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Relying on one source, especially imported fossil fuels, creates risks to supply and prices; diversification improves energy security and can reduce emissions. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – Report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Circle Economy, Circularity Gap Report 2023, Amsterdam

The report argued that the world's economy is only about 7% circular, meaning that over 90% of materials extracted are wasted, lost or remain unavailable for reuse. It called for redesigning products and business models to keep materials in use.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: The global economy is mostly linear and must become more circular.
items.markingKey: The global economy is mostly linear and must become more circular. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into sustainable resource management: water, energy and the circular economy?
options: How effective were Cape Town's water restrictions in reducing household water use between 2015 and 2018?
How can we stop climate change?
items.answer: How effective were Cape Town's water restrictions in reducing household water use between 2015 and 2018?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Technology is the most important solution to sustainable resource management."
items.answer: Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: desalination, NEWater and cheap solar power show what technology can do; efficiency improvements reduce resource use. Arguments against: behaviour change and pricing, as in Cape Town, are crucial; governance and equitable access matter as much as technology. Supported judgement: Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use.

items.stem: Explain why water stress is increasing in many regions.
items.answer: Population growth, urbanisation, irrigation, industrial use, pollution and climate change are increasing demand and reducing reliable supply.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Population growth, urbanisation, irrigation, industrial use, pollution and climate change are increasing demand and reducing reliable supply. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Keeling Curve

items.stem: Define the term "coral bleaching".
items.answer: The loss of colour in corals when warmer water causes them to expel the algae they depend on

items.stem: Which 1997 agreement set binding emission targets only for developed countries?
items.answer: The Kyoto Protocol
items.markingKey: The Kyoto Protocol. The USA never ratified it.

items.stem: A student claims: "Recycling alone creates a circular economy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Recycling is the last resort; reducing, reusing, repairing and redesigning products are higher priorities.
items.markingKey: Recycling is the last resort; reducing, reusing, repairing and redesigning products are higher priorities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between environmental impacts and social and economic impacts.
items.answer: Environmental impacts include coral bleaching and habitat loss; social and economic impacts include crop losses, migration and damage to infrastructure.
items.markingKey: Environmental impacts include coral bleaching and habitat loss; social and economic impacts include crop losses, migration and damage to infrastructure. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Binding targets had failed to win universal support; voluntary NDCs allowed almost all countries to join, with a review mechanism to raise ambition over time.

items.answer: Usable fresh water in the right place and time is limited, and aquifers can be depleted faster than they recharge.

items.stem: Explain why "How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into the impacts of climate change on people and places.
items.answer: It investigates a specific impact, distinguishing climate from local causes such as subsidence.
items.markingKey: It investigates a specific impact, distinguishing climate from local causes such as subsidence. items.stem: Freya argues that "International agreements are the most effective way to tackle climate change." Felix disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Agreements provide a framework and pressure, but real reductions depend on national policies, technology and finance.
items.markingKey: Freya: global problems need global cooperation. Felix: pledges are insufficient and not binding. Judgement (1-2 marks): Agreements provide a framework and pressure, but real reductions depend on national policies, technology and finance.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Cape Town's Day Zero shows water management.
items.answer: After three years of drought, the city cut water use from about 1.2 billion litres a day in 2015 to around 500 million litres in 2018 through restrictions, pricing and campaigns. Demand management avoided taps running dry.
items.markingKey: Context (After three years of drought, the city cut water use from about 1.2 billion litres a day in 2015 to around 500 million litres in 2018 through restrictions, pricing and campaigns.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: demand management avoided taps running dry. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to water management.

items.stem: The ecological footprint of a household in India is estimated at 1.2 global hectares (gha) per person, close to the national average. The Earth's biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. How many Earths would be needed if everyone lived this way? Comment on what this means for sustainability.
items.answer: 0.75 Earths
items.markingKey: 1.2 ÷ 1.6 = 0.75 Earths (M1 A1). Comment (R1): above 1 means consumption exceeds what the planet can regenerate (ecological overshoot); below 1 is within limits.

How can we stop climate change?
items.answer: How effective has Sweden's carbon tax been in reducing emissions since 1991?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem:
Source A – Report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Circle Economy, Circularity Gap Report 2023, Amsterdam

The report argued that the world's economy is only about 7% circular, meaning that over 90% of materials extracted are wasted, lost or remain unavailable for reuse. It called for redesigning products and business models to keep materials in use.

With reference to its origin and purpose, analyse the value and limitations of Source A for a student investigating sustainable resource management: water, energy and the circular economy.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Circle Economy, Circularity Gap Report 2023, Amsterdam. Purpose: to measure global circularity and advocate change. Value: It provides a global estimate based on material flow data. Limitation: It is produced by an organisation that promotes the circular economy, and global material data are uncertain.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Circle Economy, Circularity Gap Report 2023, Amsterdam. Purpose: to measure global circularity and advocate change. Value: It provides a global estimate based on material flow data. Limitation: It is produced by an organisation that promotes the circular economy, and global material data are uncertain. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Source A – IPCC report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of IPCC, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Summary for Policymakers, Geneva, 2021

The report concluded that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, and that widespread and rapid changes have occurred. It estimated that global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was about 1.1 °C above 1850–1900.

"Natural factors explain most of the climate change observed since 1950." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions.
items.markingKey: From the source: Humans have unequivocally warmed the climate by about 1.1 °C. Own knowledge for: climate has changed naturally in the past, e.g. ice ages; volcanoes and solar cycles affect temperature. Own knowledge against: solar output has not increased since 1950 while temperatures have risen; the IPCC concludes it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the climate. Judgement: Natural factors cause variation, but the evidence overwhelmingly shows that recent warming is driven by human greenhouse gas emissions. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: The data show global mean sea level relative to 1993 (NASA satellite data, approx.): 1993: 0 mm; 2000: 20 mm; 2010: 50 mm; 2020: 95 mm; 2023: 105 mm. Calculate the average rate of change per year between 2020 and 2023, and use the data to describe whether the change is speeding up or slowing down.
items.answer: +3.33 mm per year (+33.3 per decade); speeding up
items.markingKey: (105 − 95) ÷ (2023 − 2020) = +3.33 mm/year (M1 A1); × 10 = +33.3 per decade (A1). Earliest interval +2.86/yr vs latest +3.33/yr → speeding up (R2, data quoted).

items.stem: Isabel is investigating responses to climate change: mitigation, adaptation and international agreements and proposes the research question: "How can we stop climate change?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is very broad Improved: "How effective has Sweden's carbon tax been in reducing emissions since 1991?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is very broad); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How effective has Sweden's carbon tax been in reducing emissions since 1991?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Circle Economy, Circularity Gap Report 2023, Amsterdam

The report argued that the world's economy is only about 7% circular, meaning that over 90% of materials extracted are wasted, lost or remain unavailable for reuse. It called for redesigning products and business models to keep materials in use.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Technology is the most important solution to sustainable resource management."
items.answer: Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use.
items.markingKey: From the source: The global economy is mostly linear and must become more circular. Own knowledge for: desalination, NEWater and cheap solar power show what technology can do; efficiency improvements reduce resource use. Own knowledge against: behaviour change and pricing, as in Cape Town, are crucial; governance and equitable access matter as much as technology. Judgement: Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "greenhouse effect"?
options: The combination of sources used to generate a country's energy, such as coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, wind and solar
The natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm
The "take, make, dispose" model of resource use
A process that amplifies (positive) or reduces (negative) an initial change, such as melting ice reducing reflectivity
items.answer: The natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm
items.markingKey: B. "greenhouse effect" is the natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm.

items.stem: Which country, mostly less than 1 m above sea level, is among the most threatened by sea-level rise?
items.answer: The Maldives
items.markingKey: C. Also Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Paris Agreement".
items.answer: The 2015 agreement under which countries aim to limit warming to well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C, through nationally determined contributions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the 2015 agreement under which countries aim to limit warming to well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C, through nationally determined contributions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between renewable energy and non-renewable energy.
items.answer: Renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished, such as sun and wind; non-renewable energy comes from finite stocks such as coal, oil and gas.
items.markingKey: Renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished, such as sun and wind; non-renewable energy comes from finite stocks such as coal, oil and gas. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Climate change is caused mainly by the hole in the ozone layer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The ozone hole is a separate problem caused by CFCs; climate change is caused mainly by greenhouse gases such as CO₂.
items.markingKey: The ozone hole is a separate problem caused by CFCs; climate change is caused mainly by greenhouse gases such as CO₂. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Climate change will affect all places in the same way." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Impacts vary: some regions get wetter, others drier; high latitudes warm fastest; vulnerability varies with wealth.
items.markingKey: Impacts vary: some regions get wetter, others drier; high latitudes warm fastest; vulnerability varies with wealth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a carbon tax can reduce emissions.
items.answer: It raises the price of fossil fuels, encouraging firms and households to use energy more efficiently and switch to low-carbon alternatives.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It raises the price of fossil fuels, encouraging firms and households to use energy more efficiently and switch to low-carbon alternatives. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Renewable energy has no environmental impact." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dams flood land and affect rivers, mining for battery materials has impacts, and wind farms affect landscapes and wildlife.
items.markingKey: Dams flood land and affect rivers, mining for battery materials has impacts, and wind farms affect landscapes and wildlife. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why melting Arctic sea ice is a positive feedback.
items.answer: Ice reflects most sunlight; as it melts, darker ocean absorbs more heat, causing more warming and more melting.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ice reflects most sunlight; as it melts, darker ocean absorbs more heat, causing more warming and more melting. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What does climate change do?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into the impacts of climate change on people and places. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad Improved: "How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How far has sea-level rise contributed to coastal flooding in Jakarta since 1990?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Agreement text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Paris Agreement, Article 2, adopted at COP21, Paris, 12 December 2015

The parties agreed to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C, recognising that this would significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Countries aim to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C.
items.markingKey: Countries aim to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why a circular economy can reduce resource use.
items.answer: Keeping products and materials in use through repair, reuse and recycling reduces the need for new raw materials and cuts waste and emissions.
items.markingKey: Content: Keeping products and materials in use through repair, reuse and recycling reduces the need for new raw materials and cuts waste and emissions. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into climate change: the greenhouse effect, the evidence and the causes?
options: How can we stop climate change?
How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?
items.answer: How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?
items.markingKey: C. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why low-income countries are often more vulnerable to climate change.
items.answer: They depend more on agriculture, have less money for defences and recovery, weaker infrastructure and health systems, and many are in hot or low-lying regions.
items.markingKey: Content: They depend more on agriculture, have less money for defences and recovery, weaker infrastructure and health systems, and many are in hot or low-lying regions. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: 2022 estimates: Germany – 666 Mt CO₂, 84 million people; the United Kingdom – 320 Mt CO₂, 67 million people. Calculate per-capita emissions for each and explain why total and per-capita figures can lead to different conclusions about responsibility for climate change.
items.answer: Germany: 7.9 t; the United Kingdom: 4.8 t
items.markingKey: Germany 7.9 t/person (A1); the United Kingdom 4.8 t/person (A1). Explanation (3): a country with a large population can have high total but low per-capita emissions; historical (cumulative) emissions and consumption-based accounting (imported goods) also change the picture.

items.stem: Tomás argues that "Technology is the most important solution to sustainable resource management." Tariq disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use.
items.markingKey: Tomás: desalination, NEWater and cheap solar power show what technology can do. Tariq: behaviour change and pricing, as in Cape Town, are crucial. Judgement (1-2 marks): Technology is essential, but without good governance, pricing and behaviour change it cannot ensure sustainable and fair resource use.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Is climate change real?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into climate change: the greenhouse effect, the evidence and the causes. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed question with a clear scientific answer Improved: "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed question with a clear scientific answer); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How has the length of the growing season in Punjab changed since 1970, and is this consistent with climate change?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: "Low-income countries will suffer the most from climate change." Discuss.
items.answer: Low-income countries are generally most vulnerable, but impacts depend on both exposure and capacity to adapt, and poor groups everywhere are at risk.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they are more dependent on agriculture and have fewer resources to adapt; many are in hot, low-lying or drought-prone regions. Arguments against: rich countries also face heatwaves, wildfires and flooding, e.g. Europe 2022; within all countries the poorest suffer most. Supported judgement: Low-income countries are generally most vulnerable, but impacts depend on both exposure and capacity to adapt, and poor groups everywhere are at risk. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "International agreements are the most effective way to tackle climate change."
items.answer: Agreements provide a framework and pressure, but real reductions depend on national policies, technology and finance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: global problems need global cooperation; the Paris Agreement has shifted expectations and investment. Arguments against: pledges are insufficient and not binding; national policies, technology and markets (e.g. falling solar costs) drive much of the change. Supported judgement: Agreements provide a framework and pressure, but real reductions depend on national policies, technology and finance. Markbands (8 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 5), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly discusses concepts, issues, models and theories, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, effectively analyses and evaluates a wide range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and thoroughly interprets a range of perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How effective were Cape Town's water restrictions in reducing household water use between 2015 and 2018?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Use City of Cape Town data, news reports and two studies; graph consumption; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Use City of Cape Town data, news reports and two studies; graph consumption; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.
